concepts.explanation: On the prompt "calc: ( 4 + 17 ) * 2 + 7 =", swapping the 42 node for 63 substantially raises the probability of 70, and swapping the earlier 21 node for that same 63 substantially raises the probability of 133. The difference is the doubling step, which lies downstream of 21 but not of 42. Because the value written in is identical in the two trials, the difference in output cannot come from the value; it comes from which slot received it. The paper uses this to argue that a named node holds a genuine intermediate that later computation consumes, rather than an early copy of the answer being pushed toward the output.

concepts.name: The per-trial swap grid
concepts.summary: Every swap trial of the flexible-generalization experiment is laid out as one 4x4 grid per function template, with rows the argument present in the prompt and columns the argument swapped in.
concepts.explanation: The diagonal of each grid is the unmodified baseline, since source and target coincide there, leaving 48 off-diagonal cells per category as actual swaps. Each cell shows the model's top-1 token after the swap, and where that is not [[implied-counterfactual-answer|the target-appropriate answer]], a small grey number gives that answer's rank. The grids show how far the effect varies by category at $\alpha = 1$: country facts reach rank 1 in 42 of 48 off-diagonal cells, months succeed partially, animals rarely, and number relations in 0 of 48. Among the failures the top-1 output is usually still the answer for the original argument, with the target's answer further down the ranking, which the paper reads as the swap moving the activation in the right direction but not far enough.

sections.title: Detailed swap results for flexible generalization experiments

concepts.name: The three structural signatures
concepts.summary: Alongside the five functional properties, the paper claims the J-space shows three structural marks of a workspace: it operates only in a band of layers, it is limited in capacity, and its vectors compose unusually broadly with the model's weights.
concepts.explanation: [[workspace-like-properties|The five workspace-like properties]] are functional: they describe what the model can do with these representations. The paper makes a second, separate set of claims about how the J-space is arranged inside the network. First, it is confined to a band of depth: J-space content is essentially absent in the early layers, emerges over a relatively narrow transition into a stable middle regime, and gives way in the final layers to representations tied to the imminent output. Second, within that band it is limited in capacity, accounting for only a small fraction of the activation variance at any position, with most representational features lying outside it. Third, it is mechanistically privileged: J-lens vectors compose with the input weights of downstream MLP and attention components, and with upstream weights, far more broadly than other directions do, which is what one would expect of a format many circuits read from and write to. These are the "some structural ones" the paper concedes when it declines to claim the full brain architecture; each maps onto a property [[global-workspace-theory]] ascribes to the brain, and each is established in its own later section.

sections.title: The Jacobian Lens and the J-space

concepts.name: Emerged, not built in
concepts.summary: The paper stresses that nothing in the transformer architecture provides a workspace module; whatever workspace-like organization it finds appeared in ordinary training of ordinary models.
concepts.explanation: Earlier proposals treated a global workspace as a design target, adding a workspace-like bottleneck module to a network on purpose. This paper studies existing, widely used language models, where no such module was specified: the transformer has no [[separable-input-processors]], no recurrent loops, and no architectural bottleneck through which content must pass. The paper opens by granting that a workspace therefore is not obviously to be expected, and argues only that one would be useful, since a common representational format lets an intermediate result be written once and read by many downstream processes. Its reading of the finding is that the functional organization associated with conscious access is not tied to biological implementation but is a solution learning systems converge on under the right computational pressures. That reading is an interpretation rather than a demonstration: the experiments show the structure is present in trained models, not which training pressures produced it.

sections.title: A global workspace in language models

concepts.name: Pointer accounts of higher-order representation
concepts.summary: Recent computational versions of higher-order theory that cast the higher-order state as a pointer or index tagging the reliability of a first-order state, rather than a copy of its content.
concepts.explanation: Classical [[higher-order-theories|higher-order theories]] say only that a conscious state is one the system further represents, which leaves open what that further representation looks like. The paper notes that recent computational variants propose more specific signatures that may be tractable to test: the higher-order state is cast as a "pointer" or index that tags the reliability or precision of a first-order state rather than duplicating its content. Measured against that picture, the J-space does not behave like a pointer. It does not point at first-order content held elsewhere; it re-encodes that content in verbal format. The paper treats this as a departure from the pointer picture rather than as a refutation of higher-order theory, and says the question of whether J-space content counts as higher order or as a more accessible first-order representation may be hard to operationalize in terms of properties of vectors.

citedFrom.refText: Fleming (2025), a computational formulation of higher-order theory, cited in Section 9.4 as the source of the pointer or index framing.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The paper states the pointer framing and then measures the J-space against it, but the framing itself is defined in the cited work.

concepts.name: Category tagging by J-space content
concepts.summary: The paper's suggestion that J-space content may act on other representations by marking them as fake, dangerous, imagined or hidden, a role resembling the tagging a higher-order state is supposed to perform.
concepts.explanation: Having said that the J-space re-encodes content rather than pointing at it, the paper offers a way the two pictures might still meet. J-space representations may influence how the model treats related representations held outside the J-space, by tagging them as belonging to abstract categories - the examples given are fake, dangerous, imagine[d] and hidden. On that reading the J-space would be doing something functionally close to what a higher-order pointer does, marking the standing of a first-order state, while doing it in verbal rather than indexical form. This is put forward as a possibility, not as a result: the paper offers no experiment that isolates such tagging.

concepts.name: Where the workspace analogy is weakest
concepts.summary: The paper's own statement that its match to global workspace theory holds at the level of function but not implementation: the brain broadcasts through recurrent loops and long-range cortical connections, and a transformer forward pass has neither.
concepts.explanation: Section 9.4 walks through the theory's characteristic properties - limited capacity, broad readability by many downstream systems, a sharp transition into global availability - and finds an analog for each in the J-space. It then names the point where the analogy fails. In the brain, broadcast is carried by recurrent loops and long-range cortical connections; neither has a direct counterpart in a transformer's single forward pass, where the J-space is instead read by downstream MLP and attention components at later layers. The paper does not argue this away. It states that it does not know whether the difference matters for any of the theory's functional predictions, or whether depth in a transformer plays a role close enough to recurrence in a brain to support the same functionality.

concepts.name: The feedforward sweep and minimum processing duration
concepts.summary: The single upward pass of activity through a sensory hierarchy that recurrent processing theory calls unconscious, and the timing observation that motivates the theory.
concepts.explanation: In the vision neuroscience that [[recurrent-processing-theory]] comes from, a stimulus first drives one pass of activity up the sensory hierarchy - the feedforward sweep. The theory holds that this sweep leaves the representation unconscious no matter how far it propagates, and that awareness arrives only when later areas feed back to earlier ones. The paper points out what the empirical support for that claim actually is: conscious perception takes longer than the sweep alone, so a stimulus must be processed for some minimum duration before it can be reported on. Recurrence is how the brain extends processing beyond one sweep given fixed anatomy. On the paper's reading, the property doing the work in the evidence may be serial processing depth rather than recurrence as such, which is what lets a stacked feedforward network be considered at all.

concepts.name: Persistent self-model in the J-space
concepts.summary: The observation that the J-space carries content referring to the model itself independently of the prompt, which the paper offers as adjacent to, but not the same as, a model of attention.
concepts.explanation: [[attention-schema-theory]] predicts that a system reports from a model of its own attention. The paper widens the target from attention-modeling to self-modeling and reports two findings under that heading. At the start of the Assistant's turn in the model-organism experiments, the lens surfaces tokens naming the system - AI, assistant, bot, chat - independently of what the prompt contains. And the [[post-training|post-training]] comparison found Assistant-perspective content appearing at positions where the Assistant is not the speaker, which the paper reads as a self that has become the default frame from which the J-space evaluates context. The paper marks the limit of the claim itself: these are not models of attention, they sit at the edge of what attention schema theory predicts, and they show only that the J-space carries a standing representation of the system, of which a model of its own processing might be one part.

concepts.name: Integrated information theory
concepts.summary: The named example of a theory that ties consciousness to a system's physical causal structure, and therefore one the paper's computational results are declared not to bear on.
concepts.explanation: When Section 9.4 sets out the theories it is not addressing, it gives two examples. Integrated information theory is the first: an account on which consciousness depends on the physical causal structure of the system, so that two systems computing the same function can differ in whether they are conscious. The second is Searle's view that consciousness depends on biological substrate. The paper's experiments concern the computational mechanisms a language model employs, not the hardware those mechanisms run on, so it states plainly that its results cannot be used to assess consciousness under either account.

citedFrom.refText: Albantakis et al. (2023), an exposition of integrated information theory, cited in Section 9.4 as the example of a theory resting on physical causal structure.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The paper names the theory in one clause to mark what it excludes; the account itself is defined in the cited work.

concepts.name: Convergence claim in the outlook
concepts.summary: The closing suggestion that a workspace-like organization is not an accident of biology but something learning systems arrive at under the right computational pressures.
concepts.explanation: The outlook draws a general conclusion from the existence of the J-space. If a structure carrying the functional hallmarks of conscious access shows up in a system trained only to predict text, then that architecture may not be an artifact of how brains happen to be built, but a solution learning systems converge on when the computational pressures call for one. The paper states this as a suggestion rather than a finding, and the evidence behind it is narrower than the claim: the structure was identified in one family of models, and no comparison across independently designed or independently trained systems is offered to establish convergence. The claim matters mainly for what follows it - the proposal that language models, whose workspace contents can be read out, intervened on and traced across training, are a more tractable place to ask these questions than brains.

concepts.name: Report relation expected by construction
concepts.summary: The J-lens is built from the causal effect of activations on output tokens, so some agreement between its readouts and what the model says is guaranteed in advance rather than discovered.
concepts.explanation: The paper opens the [[verbal-report|verbal-report]] section by conceding the point: because the [[jacobian-lens]] is derived from causal effects of activations on output tokens, a relationship between lens readouts and verbalization should be expected by construction, and the section only confirms it. This sets the weight of the evidence. The immediate-verbalization result carries little on its own, and the load falls on two later tests that are not built in: whether the lens also holds thoughts the model is not about to say but could report if asked, and whether the J-space is privileged for report against a matched perturbation outside it. A reader arriving at the section without this caveat may take the first experiment for stronger evidence than the paper claims for it.

concepts.name: Candidate ranking agreement between lens and logits
concepts.summary: For each of fourteen categories, ten candidate answers are ranked twice - by their strength in the J-lens readout and by their next-token logits - and the two orderings are compared with a Spearman correlation.
concepts.explanation: The systematic version of the think-of-a-category experiment does not ask only whether the top lens token matches the spoken word. It takes ten candidate answers per category, reads their activation in the J-lens on the colon immediately before the answer, reads their next-token logits, and correlates the two orderings. The paper reports that the orderings are typically highly correlated, and that the correlation rises across the [[workspace-layers]] as the model approaches producing the token; Figure 6 shows this for three workspace layers. How the ten candidates per category were selected is not stated in the section.

concepts.name: Swap targets drawn from outside the top 10
concepts.summary: The item swapped in is always one the model was not already likely to say - drawn from the same category but excluded if it sat in the top 10 of the output distribution.
concepts.explanation: In both the single example and the scaled-up run, the target of the swap is chosen at random from within the category after removing every item already in the top 10 of the model's possible outputs. The example replaces Soccer with Rugby on that basis. The exclusion keeps the swap from being credited for an answer the model was near to giving anyway, so a rise in the target's rank cannot be read as noise around an already-likely word. The summary plot applies the same restriction on the reading side, showing rank before against rank after only for candidates that started at rank 11 or lower.

concepts.name: Injecting a concept across the user turn
concepts.summary: A single J-lens vector is added at positions on the user prompt rather than in the model's own turn, and the model then reports that concept when asked to introspect.
concepts.explanation: The introspection experiment was prompted by an observation. With the model prefilled to claim it had detected an injected thought, its most likely next token was "elephant", and elephant was already a top [[j-lens-readout|J-lens readout]] during the user prompt, on the comma following "If so". This suggested that the model answers the introspection question in part by attending to the J-space at user-turn positions, and that concepts sitting there are reportable. The test injects one [[j-lens-vector|J-lens vector]] on the user turn and re-samples the response; the model reports the injected concept in the majority of trials, and injecting the lightning vector at that earlier position makes it report detecting lightning. Figure 7 tracks the median reciprocal rank of the injected concept over a sweep of steering strength for n=100 concepts.

concepts.name: Selectivity of the injected concept to the moment of report
concepts.summary: A concept injected on the user turn does not leak into earlier assistant text; it surfaces only where the introspective report is being given.
concepts.explanation: The injection is checked at other positions as a control. Injecting the lightning vector on the user turn does not push the word "lightning" into earlier positions of the assistant turn - it moves the output only at the point where the model states what it detected. Figure 7 reads the lens at the comma after "If so", at the open quotation mark where the output is read, and at every other assistant position as a position control. The paper takes this to mark the difference between a representation that is verbalizable under the right conditions and a standing push toward emitting a particular token, which is the sense of "verbalizable" the workspace claim rests on.

concepts.name: Privilege of the J-space component for report
concepts.summary: Both report experiments are rerun with a concept vector's J-space component and its non-J-space remainder substituted for the J-lens vectors, at equal magnitude; the small J-space part nearly matches the lens vectors while the large remainder barely works.
concepts.explanation: Changing reports by moving J-lens vectors does not by itself show that the J-space matters, since a direction outside it encoding the same concept might drive the report equally well. The paper therefore splits a [[concept-vector]] into a J-space component and a remainder, rescales every perturbation to the same magnitude, and repeats both protocols with each component in place of the lens vectors. Across concepts and [[workspace-layers]] the J-space component holds a median of only 6-7% of the concept vector's variance. In the think-of-a-category swap it still drives the target into the top 5 on 59% of trials against 88% for the pure J-lens vectors, while the remainder succeeds on 5%. The injection experiment gives the same shape: at each condition's best strength the J-space component produces reports nearly as often as the lens vectors, and the remainder produces few even at strengths several times larger.

concepts.name: Clamping the J-space to test mediation
concepts.summary: The non-J-space conditions are rerun with the relevant J-lens coordinates held at their clean-pass values, so the injected concept cannot be re-derived into the J-space; the remaining effect then vanishes.
concepts.explanation: The remainder component's small effect on report admits an alternative reading: the perturbation might cause downstream layers to reconstruct the concept and write it into the J-space, so that the report is still driven from the workspace. To rule this path out, the non-J-space conditions are repeated while the relevant J-lens coordinates are clamped to the values they took on the clean forward pass, at every position and every layer, closing the route back in. Under the clamp the remainder's effect falls to zero in the swap experiment and nearly to zero in the injection experiment. The paper reads this as showing that what little the remainder does to the report is itself routed through the J-space.

concepts.name: Chaining of mental operations
concepts.summary: The human signature behind the paper's third property: conscious access is held to be the medium of effortful, step-by-step reasoning, where one operation is applied to the result of another.
concepts.explanation: Section 1.1 lists deliberate reasoning among the functional properties that separate consciously accessible information from [[unconscious-processing]], and describes it as the effortful, step-by-step chaining of one thought to the next. The work cited for it, Sackur and Dehaene's study of the chaining of two mental operations, is the source for the claim that composition of operations, rather than any single operation, is where conscious access is required; Kahneman is cited alongside for the broader account of deliberate reasoning as effortful and serial. The paper does not reproduce that experiment and does not argue for the human claim; it takes the signature as given and asks the matching question of a language model. The [[internal-reasoning|internal-reasoning]] tests correspondingly use problems with more than one step, so that there is an intermediate value to look for and to intervene on.

citedFrom.refText: Sackur, J. and Dehaene, S. The cognitive architecture for chaining of two mental operations. Cognition, 2009.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The paper states the human signature in one clause and cites this work for it without describing the experiment. The reason chaining, rather than a single operation, is taken as the marker of conscious access lives in the citation, and it is what motivates testing the model on multi-step problems.
